assessment.nobel_worthiness: The magic-wavelength optical lattice clock combines Doppler- and recoil-free spectroscopy of many atoms with extreme precision, and it is a genuine conceptual step beyond single-ion clocks. It has opened the way to redefining the second, to relativistic geodesy and to tests of fundamental constants. For a theorist who values quantitative agreement between theory and experiment, this is the cleanest case.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and led its first realisation in strontium. Ye's group brought the clocks to the 10^-18 level and made the many-body and density-dependent studies. The two-person credit is a natural configuration; other groups (e.g. Lemonde, Gill, Lisdat) contributed but the core concept is cleanly attributable. As far as I recall.
assessment.maturity: Independently reproduced by several laboratories worldwide, with clocks now compared across continents and the redefinition of the SI second under discussion. The recognition is timely and the interpretation is stable.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wishes to honour clocks together with Wineland and Haroche 2012 (ion clocks) or regards this as an incremental extension.
Ye also appears in the ultracold-molecule candidate, so any combined configuration needs care.
I have not verified priority details among Katori, Ye and others from the primary papers.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Loading ultracold atoms into optical lattices to realise the Hubbard model, with the observed superfluid to Mott insulator transition and later single-site quantum-gas microscopes, gives a controllable laboratory for many-body physics. It tells us something new about how matter behaves when interactions are tuned at will. This is fundamental, reproduced science with wide reach.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and collaborators (Jaksch, Cirac and others) proposed the lattice Hubbard realisation, while Greiner and Bloch demonstrated the Mott transition and later developed microscopy. Cirac and Dalibard are also credited and are strong, so choosing three is a real compromise and the allocation is unresolved. I proposed Bloch, Greiner and Zoller as theory plus the two principal experimentalists, but this is a judgement.
assessment.maturity: Twenty years of replication in many groups, with quantum-gas microscopes and quantum simulation now routine. The field is mature, although the prize-worthy discovery is perhaps spread over a long programme.
uncertainties: Overlap with the Cirac-Zoller trapped-ion candidates and the Rydberg-array candidate, and the risk of splitting credit between candidates.
Whether Greiner's Mott-insulator experiment should be credited with Bloch and Hänsch, who are not in the credited names.
Four or five claimants cannot fit in a three-person prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution turns the no-cloning property and entanglement into a practical cryptographic primitive. It is a clear conceptual invention that follows on from the 2022 Bell-test prize and has been demonstrated over fibre and satellite links. It is of high conceptual originality, though it is also technologically motivated.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) and Ekert (E91, entanglement-based) are the three standard names, and this is a natural trio. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea and Experimental pioneers are a possible complication.
assessment.maturity: The protocols date from 1984 and 1991 and have been implemented repeatedly. The security proofs are established, while practical device-security issues remain in the real world. Recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as physics or as computer science and cryptography.
Wiesner's prior contribution and the role of experimental demonstrators.
Practical security of implementations is not fully settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms is a precision tool that measures gravity, rotation and fundamental constants, and it tests the equivalence principle. It demonstrates the wave nature of whole atoms in a way that is conceptually satisfying and quantitatively demanding.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard (first atom interferometers, optical gratings), Bordé (the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer theory) and Kasevich (light-pulse gravimeters and gyroscopes) are widely recognised. Chu, who already shared the 1997 prize, and Chu's role complicate the picture. The three names form a defensible configuration.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with commercial gravimeters and long-baseline tests under way. The key results have been reproduced worldwide, although several headline applications are still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with Chu's earlier laureate work on laser cooling and Ramsey-type separated-field methods (Ramsey 1989).
Priority between Bordé and the American groups is something I cannot fully adjudicate from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and Blatt's experimental realisation of gates, entanglement and algorithms established a leading platform for quantum computing. It is important and original, and follows naturally on the 2012 prize for ion control.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the theory originators and Blatt is a leading experimental realiser, but Wineland (already a laureate) and Monroe also did decisive experimental work. The three-person configuration is plausible but the experimental credit is not fully clean.
assessment.maturity: Well reproduced across several groups and now in industrial development. Timing is reasonable, but it competes with the optical-lattice candidate for the same theorists.
uncertainties: Cirac and Zoller are also credited in the lattice-simulation candidate, so the same theorists cannot be rewarded twice in a sensible slate.
Experimental credit relative to Wineland and Monroe is unclear.
Scalability and the overall importance of quantum computing remain open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry's geometric phase show that phases and potentials, not only forces, carry physical meaning in quantum mechanics. This is about as fundamental as it gets and the ideas ripple through optics, molecules and condensed matter, including topological phases.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959) is the original, but Bohm died in 1992 and cannot be recognised, so Aharonov is alone for that part. Berry (1984) is clear for the geometric phase, with Pancharatnam and Longuet-Higgins as precursors. The two-name configuration pairs two related but distinct discoveries, so it is a compound candidate.
assessment.maturity: Both effects have been confirmed many times, but this is very old, and a prize may now look overdue rather than timely. The interpretation is stable.
uncertainties: Compound discovery: the Aharonov-Bohm effect and the Berry phase may deserve different treatment.
Bohm's deceased status and precursors such as Ehrenberg-Siday and Pancharatnam.
Whether the committee would feel it is too late or too foundational.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling and controlling molecules down to the ultracold regime, including buffer-gas cooling, laser cooling of molecules and chemistry in a controlled quantum regime, opens precision tests such as the electron electric dipole moment. This is a real frontier of AOMD physics, and I can appreciate its difficulty, although it is a less settled discovery than clocks.
assessment.attribution: DeMille, Doyle and Ye all made decisive contributions (buffer-gas beams, laser cooling, eEDM and Stark-decelerated molecules), although Ni, Jin and others also built ultracold KRb molecules. Jin has died and Ye is also in the clock candidate, so the allocation is not simple.
assessment.maturity: Still developing. Laser-cooled molecules and eEDM bounds are reproduced, but the field is perhaps a few years from the point where a clear single discovery stands out.
uncertainties: Premature relative to clocks and lattice simulation.
The credit for ultracold polar molecules (Jin, Ni, Ye) versus laser-cooled molecules (DeMille, Doyle) is fragmented.
Ye's other candidacy.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling a mechanical object to its quantum ground state and entangling or squeezing it asks the question I care about, where the boundary between the quantum and classical worlds lies. It follows thematically from the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling, but it is a different system and a different insight.
assessment.attribution: Cleland and Martinis showed the ground state of a mechanical resonator, Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer developed the cavity optomechanical cooling and quantum control. Teufel, Painter, Schwab and others are also strong, so credit is spread across many groups.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced in several platforms, but the field is still young and its main discovery is less crisp. A recent related prize in 2025 may make the committee cautious about timing.
uncertainties: Possible overlap in theme with the 2025 prize.
Credit is distributed across many equal groups.
The unique decisive discovery is not clear.
